title: Wild Goats, Wild Donkeys, and the War Horse
summary: God continues his first speech with a gallery of animals. He asks Job whether he knows when the mountain goats give birth, who set the wild donkey free, whether the wild ox will serve him, why the ostrich behaves as she does, who gave the war horse its courage, and whether the hawk and eagle fly at Job's command. Each creature lives by a wisdom and a freedom that God gave it and that Job neither made nor controls.
story: The chapter continues without a break from chapter 38, where God began his answer to Job out of the whirlwind. Chapter 38 ranged over the earth, sea, sky, and stars and ended with the lion and the raven. Now the focus narrows to animals, most of them wild creatures that live beyond human reach. The speech is still made of questions, and it still says nothing about Job's suffering or the test of the prologue. At the end of the chapter God will pause and demand a reply, and in 40:3-5 Job will answer briefly, laying his hand over his mouth. Then God will speak again, turning to Behemoth and Leviathan.
historical:
The animals in the chapter belong to the natural world of the ancient Near East, and most were familiar to people in and around Israel. The mountain goat is the ibex, which still lives in the rocky hills near the Dead Sea around En Gedi. The wild donkey (the onager) roamed the steppe and desert fringes. The wild ox, the re'em, is usually identified with the aurochs, the great wild cattle of Europe and the Near East that are now extinct; Assyrian kings hunted them and depicted them in reliefs. The ostrich once lived in the deserts of Arabia and the Levant, though that population has since died out.

The war horse described in verses 19 to 25 reflects the military world of the second and first millennia BC, when horses pulled chariots and later carried mounted troops. Horses were costly military assets, associated with the great powers of Egypt and Mesopotamia, and Israel's law warned its kings against multiplying them (Deuteronomy 17:16). The ram's horn trumpet, the shofar, was used to signal battle.
cultural:
Almost every creature God mentions is one that human beings cannot tame or use. In the ancient world, as now, people valued animals mainly for what they could do: the donkey carried loads, the ox plowed, the horse went to war. God deliberately picks the wild versions. The wild donkey scorns the city and the driver's shouts (verse 7); the wild ox will not stay by the manger or pull the plow (verses 9 to 12). Their freedom is God's gift, and they belong to him, not to any human master.

The ostrich passage (verses 13 to 18) is humorous. The bird appears foolish: she lays her eggs on the ground and seems careless of them, and God says he has deprived her of wisdom. Yet she outruns the horse and its rider. The description reflects how ostriches looked to ancient observers, who saw eggs left in shallow scrapes in the sand; modern naturalists note that ostriches are more attentive to their nests than the poem suggests. The point isn't zoology but delight: God made a creature that is ridiculous and magnificent at the same time.
literary: The chapter is a catalog arranged mostly in pairs of creatures: mountain goat and doe, wild donkey and wild ox, ostrich and horse, hawk and eagle. Each portrait begins with a question to Job (Do you know? Who set free? Will he consent? Do you give?) and then describes the animal in vivid detail. The war horse portrait is among the most admired passages of Hebrew poetry, full of sound and motion: pawing, snorting, laughing at fear, catching the scent of battle. The chapter closes on a stark image, the eagle's young feasting on blood where the slain lie. God's world is not tame, and the speech doesn't pretend it is.

outline.t: The mountain goats and deer give birth
The wild ox that will not serve

doctrines.note: Each animal is God's work, made with its own nature, habitat, and strengths. God made the wilderness the wild donkey's home and gave the horse its might. Creation is diverse, wild, and valued by God for its own sake.

God knows when the mountain goats give birth, guides the hawk's migration south, and sets the eagle's nest on the crag. His care extends to creatures that live entirely outside human knowledge or control.

God gives wisdom and understanding, and he withholds them from the ostrich. Even what looks like foolishness in creation lies within God's design. Human wisdom begins by acknowledging how little of this design we see or govern.

words.note: Reem, wild ox, usually identified with the aurochs, the powerful and untamable wild cattle of the ancient world. The Greek translation rendered it with a word meaning one-horned creature, which is why older English versions such as the King James have unicorn. Its strength is the point: Job can't harness it.

Renen, ostrich, a word found only here and related to a verb for crying out, perhaps after the bird's loud call. The ostrich portrait is the one place in the speech where God describes a creature as lacking wisdom, and yet she laughs at the horse and rider.

Nesher, usually translated eagle, though many scholars think it often refers to the griffon vulture, which fits verse 30: where the slain are, there he is. The bird appears across Scripture as a picture of strength, speed, and God's care (Exodus 19:4, Isaiah 40:31).

Pere, wild donkey or onager. It lives in the salt flats and the wilderness and scorns the city. Genesis 16:12 uses the word to describe Ishmael's untamed life. Here it stands for freedom that God himself has granted.

christ: This chapter isn't a prophecy of Christ, and it shouldn't be read as allegory. Its connection to the story that leads to Jesus is thematic. The God who knows when the mountain goats give birth and watches the hawk's flight is the God Jesus described when he said that not one sparrow falls to the ground apart from the Father's care, and that his disciples are worth more than many sparrows (Matthew 10:29-31). The chapter shows a creator who delights in creatures and sustains them without needing them. In the New Testament that same creator enters his creation as a man, and Paul says that the whole creation, now groaning, waits to be set free when God's children are revealed (Romans 8:19-22). The wildness of this chapter belongs to a world God intends to heal, not to discard.

hard.q: Why does God speak about animals, including an eagle feeding on the slain, when Job is grieving his children?
hard.a:
The speech can seem strangely unrelated to Job's pain, and its last image seems harsh. Interpreters have offered several responses. One is that God is enlarging Job's world: Job has measured everything by his own suffering and by the question of whether he was treated justly, and God shows him a creation so vast and varied that no single human life can serve as its measure. Another is that the animals, especially the wild ones, show a world that runs by God's wisdom rather than by human categories of reward and punishment; the eagle feeding on the slain is not moral or immoral, simply part of a world that includes death.

A third reading notes the tenderness in the speech. God watches the goats in labor and counts their months, and he knows when the young ones leave home. For a man who lost all his children, that attention is not irrelevant. The speech doesn't comfort Job with explanations, but it shows him a God who sees and cares for what no one else sees.

questions: God points to creatures that humans can't tame or use. What does their freedom suggest about how God values things that are no use to us?
The ostrich is both foolish and magnificent. Where do you see that same mixture in people, including yourself, and how might God see it?
God asks whether the hawk flies by Job's understanding. What parts of your life have you tried to control that belong to God's wisdom instead?
